overview.text: Powhatan, often identified by his personal name Wahunsenacawh (also spelled Wahunsunacock), was the mamanatowick, or paramount chief, of Tsenacomoco, the Powhatan chiefdom in Tidewater Virginia. By the English arrival at Jamestown in 1607, he had expanded an inherited core of six tribes through diplomacy and force; roughly 28–32 tribes or chiefdoms paid him tribute. His authority was powerful but not absolute, since local chiefs and councils retained roles. Werowocomoco served as his principal residence and political center. He managed relations with English colonists through negotiation and exchange as well as resistance to their growing presence. Pocahontas was his daughter. His leadership made him central to Virginia’s earliest English-colonial encounters; his death was reported in 1618.

key_facts.text: Mamanatowick was the title for Tsenacomoco’s paramount chief; Powhatan held that role when the English arrived in 1607.
Tsenacomoco covered much of Tidewater Virginia, from the James River north toward the Potomac, with boundaries that shifted with Powhatan’s influence.
Powhatan inherited a core of six tribes and extended his influence through diplomacy and force; local chiefs and councils also held political roles.
The famous account of Pocahontas saving John Smith comes from Smith’s account; scholars have debated how to interpret the event.
Powhatan’s death was reported in 1618; after his death, leadership passed first to his brother or kinsman Opitchapam.
